Great question! Here's a summary of the paper.

## The core argument

Lovett borrows Hardin's 1968 idea of the Tragedy of the Commons, but uses it for its structure rather than its fatalism. The paper argues that AI-era work needs two kinds of expertise: **Internalized Mastery**, which is deep domain knowledge built through deliberate practice, and **Distributed Mastery**, which is fluency in orchestrating human-AI systems. Because the second depends on the first, organizations that stop training juniors may eventually lose the ability to check AI output at all.

## The evidence

- Workers ages 22 to 25 experienced a 16% relative decline in employment between October 2022 and September 2025 in the most AI-exposed occupations.
- Employment for older workers in those same occupations fell by roughly 8% over the same period.
- In one study, most participants spotted errors in AI recommendations but kept following the advice anyway.
- The paper was funded by a grant from the National Science Foundation.

## Implications

The author concludes that this tragedy is inevitable no matter what organizations do. Instead, the paper calls on HRD to treat expertise as a shared resource that needs governance at the level of the profession, not just individual firms. Lovett also recommends that Congress pass a federal apprenticeship mandate for AI-exposed industries.
